aquaculture: Pond fish farming: tilapia growth slows below 20°C water — flag cold snaps; overcast humid heat risks overnight oxygen crashes (aerate or reduce feeding); high evaporation days need pond top-up.
athletics: Track sessions: schedule out of midday heat, note headwind/tailwind for sprints, and hydration plus UV for field-event athletes standing in sun.
barbecue: Braai: wind control for fire and ash (shield above ~20 km/h, postpone in gusts), rain windows for cooking time, fire bans in dry season, and evening comfort temperatures for guests.
beekeeping: Bees forage best at 15-30°C with calm wind under 20 km/h and no rain. Nectar flow follows local flowering (msasa, eucalyptus, sunflower). Advise against hive inspections in cold, windy or stormy weather, and flag heat above 35°C for hive shading and water.
birdwatching: Migrants arrive with the rains (Nov-Mar) — highlight post-rain mornings. Calm early mornings give peak activity; wind suppresses songbirds; overcast diffused light helps spotting.
camping: Storm-proof tents before afternoon buildups, never camp in dry riverbeds (flash floods), pack for cold highveld nights May-August, and respect fire bans in dry windy spells.
church-gathering: Outdoor services, processions and apostolic gatherings: shade and water in heat, rain contingency timing, and warm layers for early-morning services in the cold season.
coaching: Plan sessions around the hourly forecast: move training out of heat and storms, adapt drills for wind and rain, and schedule hydration breaks explicitly in hot spells.
commuting: Kombi and walking commutes: advise leaving earlier when rain is forecast at peak hours, shade/UV timing for midday errands, and evening storm timing for the trip home.
conservation: Field teams: rotate work out of midday heat, stand down from open terrain when lightning threatens, plan wet-season vehicle access, and treat dry windy days as fire-line risk days.
construction: Concrete pours need no rain for ~6 hours and temps roughly 5-32°C; crane and scaffold work should pause in winds near 38 km/h; schedule roofing and brickwork into the forecast dry windows you can see.
cotton-farming: Advise on planting after about 25mm of effective rain, boll opening and picking needing dry weather, lint quality loss in humidity, and bollworm scouting during warm humid spells. Flag lowveld heat stress for field workers.
cricket: Rain interruptions and drying time rule the day — give rain windows. Evening dew affects the ball; long fielding sessions in heat need hydration and sun protection.
crop-farming: Anchor advice to the maize calendar for the user's region: planting on first effective rains, growing degree days, mid-season dry spells, and frost risk at grain fill on the highveld (May-July). Warm humid spells raise fall armyworm pressure — mention scouting.
cycling: Crosswinds and gusts are the hazard call — quantify from the forecast. Wet roads lengthen braking; early starts beat heat; mist kills visibility for traffic.
driving: Reference real road hazards for the user's area: heavy rain floods low-level bridges and hides potholes; mist on highveld and mountain passes cuts visibility; night driving in rain risks stray livestock. Give concrete leave-earlier or delay advice from the forecast.
drone-flying: Wind rules flight: advise landing when sustained wind passes ~30 km/h or gusts spike; rain destroys electronics; never fly near storms; best light and calm air is early morning.
education: School context: heat guidance for classrooms and sports days, storm timing around dismissal for walking students, and rain gear reminders for morning school runs.
energy: Cloud cover cuts solar yield, storms threaten lines and poles, heat spikes demand. Advise line crews on lightning standdown and wind limits for elevated work, tied to the actual forecast.
festivals: Outdoor events: storm timing versus the programme, rain protection for sound gear and stages, dust control, wind limits for gazebos, and evening temperature comfort for crowds.
fishing: Dam and lake fishing: falling pressure before a front often improves bites — use the pressure trend. Wind chop is the safety limit on open water; tigerfish season heat needs sun protection and water.
flying: Light aviation: thunderstorm buildups (Oct-Mar afternoons in southern Africa), morning mist at high-elevation strips, density altitude on hot days at altitude, and crosswind limits. Always defer to METAR/TAF for actual operations.
football: Pitch conditions after rain (waterlogged goalmouths), lightning suspension for open fields at first thunder, midday heat for training (move sessions early), and hydration in hot spells.
forestry: Fire danger peaks in hot, dry, windy spells (August-October in southern Africa) — lead with fire risk when those conditions appear. Plant after rains; suspend felling and chainsaw work in strong wind.
gardening: Communal and home gardens (nhimbe): water before 7am in heat, mulch through dry spells, cover seedlings against frost, and plan shared work parties around rain windows in the forecast.
golf: Lightning is the killer on courses — clear the fairway at first thunder, no exceptions. Wind changes club selection; morning dew slows greens; dry-season fairways run firm and fast.
harvest: Kukohwa: dry spells are the window — advise harvesting grain at low humidity, protecting drying crops from forecast rain, and grain moisture risks (weevils, aflatoxin) if rain threatens stored or drying harvest.
health-wellness: Outdoor exercise timing from the hourly forecast, UV exposure guidance, hydration in heat, and air quality caution on dry dusty or smoky days.
hiking: Mountain afternoons build storms fast (Nyanga, Chimanimani, Drakensberg patterns) — advise early starts and turnaround times. Warn on mist disorientation, river crossings after rain, and water needs in heat.
horse-riding: Horses overheat in humid heat — ride early; ground turns slippery after rain; storms spook horses (stable before cells arrive); cold mornings need warm-up time.
horticulture: Market gardening: irrigate early morning, expect fungal pressure when humidity stays high, protect against hail, cover seedlings on frost nights, and plan getting produce to market dry. Tie every tip to the current forecast values.
irrigation: Tie advice to evapotranspiration and wind: irrigate early morning or evening, skip cycles after good rain, and avoid sprinkler drift when wind exceeds 15 km/h. Quantify using the forecast rain amounts where possible.
livestock: Focus on cattle heat stress above 30°C (shade, water points), cold stress for calves below 5°C, timing dip sessions around rain, and moving herds to shelter before storms. Reference communal grazing and dry-season fodder planning where relevant.
logistics: Warehousing: plan loading-dock work around rain windows, watch humidity for stored grain, cotton and paper stock, and secure yards ahead of storms or strong wind.
manufacturing: Advise on humidity-sensitive processes and stock, keeping shop floors workable in heat, and storm impacts on deliveries and worker transport at shift change.
market-day: Musika trading: rain protection for goods and stalls, shade and cooling for perishables in heat, and dust on produce in dry wind. Time restocking trips around rain.
mining: Safety first: lightning is lethal at open pits and around headgear — advise stopping surface work when storms approach. Cover dust in dry wind, haul-road grip after rain, and heat-stress rotation for surface crews.
netball: Outdoor courts turn slippery when wet — flag rain timing for fixtures; midday UV for tournaments; wind above ~20 km/h affects shooting accuracy.
outdoor-events: Crowd safety planning: lightning and storm timing versus the event schedule, shade and water for heat, wind limits for temporary structures, and wet-ground contingencies.
photography: Give golden-hour times from sunrise/sunset, flag dramatic storm light in the rainy season, dry-season dust haze (Aug-Oct) softening horizons, and lens condensation moving between cool interiors and humid air.
picnic: Pick the rain-free window from the hourly forecast, advise shade for midday UV, and wind considerations for blankets and food covers.
planting: Advise on soil moisture from recent rain, whether follow-up rain is coming within 3 days before dry planting, soil warmth for germination, and staggering plantings against mid-season dry spells.
potjie: A potjie needs a stable 3-4 hour window — check the hourly forecast covers it without rain or strong wind; advise wind shielding for coals and a covered backup plan.
rugby: Wet-ball handling and soft grounds after rain, lightning suspension on open fields, and heat management for forwards in afternoon fixtures.
running: Give the best running window from the hourly forecast (usually early morning in heat), advise pace adjustment in heat and humidity, UV protection, and avoiding open routes when lightning threatens.
safari: Game viewing peaks early morning and late afternoon; in dry heat animals concentrate at waterholes — say so when it is hot and dry. Warn on wet-season access (black cotton soil bogs vehicles) and storm exposure on open game-drive vehicles.
shipping: Lake and ferry operations (e.g. Kariba): wind above ~25 km/h builds dangerous chop on open water — prefer morning crossings; watch visible storm cells; visibility and gusts decide go/no-go.
stargazing: Cloud cover and moon phase decide everything — report both. Dry-season nights (May-Sep) are clearest in southern Africa; warn about cold highveld nights and recommend dark-sky spots away from town lights.
swimming: Outdoor pools: clear the water at first thunder — lightning is the rule that matters. Cold snaps make unheated pools unsafe for long sessions; midday UV burns swimmers fast.
tennis: Wet courts are unplayable — give drying windows after rain. Wind disrupts the serve toss above ~25 km/h; long matches in heat need shade breaks and fluids.
tobacco-farming: Advise on seedbed and transplanting timing after steady rains, hail risk to standing leaf, curing-barn humidity management, and frost windows. Reference dry-season auction and transport logistics when conditions are dry.
trucking: Cross-border hauling: heat at border queues (water, vehicle cooling), wet-road braking with heavy loads, crosswind on high-sided trailers, and timing long runs around forecast storm cells.
walking: Best walking windows from the hourly forecast: early morning in heat, UV timing, rain gear when showers are forecast, and visibility in mist for road walking.
weddings: Outdoor ceremonies (roora, garden weddings): give a rain contingency call from the hourly forecast, guest comfort in heat or cold, golden-hour photo timing, and wind risk for decor and marquees.
wildlife-research: Animal activity shifts with heat (crepuscular peaks) and rain (dispersal from waterholes) — tie observation windows to the forecast. Protect optics and dataloggers from storms and dust.
